source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Homomorphism factors through a quotient
statement: A group homomorphism phi:G->H factors uniquely through the canonical projection G->G/N exactly when N is contained in ker(phi).
conditions: N is a normal subgroup of G.
phi:G->H is a group homomorphism.
conclusion: There is a unique homomorphism phi_bar:G/N->H with phi=phi_bar composed with the quotient map if and only if N is contained in ker(phi).
typical_uses: Make a map on cosets well-defined.
Repair a proposed quotient homomorphism by checking representatives.
common_misuses: Defining phi_bar(gN)=phi(g) without proving N is contained in the kernel.
Claiming the induced map is injective without showing ker(phi)=N.
bridge_lemmas: If gN=hN, then h^{-1}g lies in N.
The kernel of the induced map is ker(phi)/N.
repair_templates: Prove N is contained in ker(phi), then define the induced map on cosets and verify well-definedness.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Commutator subgroup controls abelian quotients
statement: For a normal subgroup N of G, the quotient G/N is abelian exactly when the commutator subgroup G' is contained in N.
conditions: G is a group.
N is a normal subgroup of G.
G' is generated by all commutators [x,y].
conclusion: G/N is abelian if and only if G' is contained in N; in particular G/G' is abelian and is the largest abelian quotient of G.
typical_uses: Check whether a quotient is abelian.
Factor a homomorphism from G to an abelian group through the abelianization.
common_misuses: Reversing the containment and requiring N to be contained in G'.
Using G/N when N has not been shown normal.
bridge_lemmas: Cosets xN and yN commute exactly when [x,y] lies in N.
repair_templates: Reduce commutativity of arbitrary cosets to containment of every commutator in N.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Characteristic-normal transitivity rules
statement: A characteristic subgroup of a normal subgroup is normal in the whole group; a characteristic subgroup of a characteristic subgroup is characteristic.
conditions: K is characteristic in H.
For the normality conclusion, H is normal in G; for the characteristic conclusion, H is characteristic in G.
conclusion: If K char H and H normal G, then K normal G; if K char H and H char G, then K char G.
typical_uses: Supply a valid transitivity step in subgroup chains.
Prove canonical subgroups are normal in a larger group.
common_misuses: Assuming normality is transitive from K normal H and H normal G.
Replacing characteristic hypotheses by normality in the characteristic conclusion.
bridge_lemmas: Conjugation by an element of G restricts to an automorphism of H when H is normal.
repair_templates: Strengthen K normal H to K characteristic H, or prove invariance under conjugation by G directly.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Ring homomorphism factors through quotient
statement: A ring homomorphism phi:R->S induces a unique homomorphism R/I->S exactly when I is contained in ker(phi).
conditions: I is a two-sided ideal of R.
phi:R->S is a ring homomorphism.
conclusion: The rule r+I maps to phi(r) defines a unique induced ring homomorphism precisely when I is contained in ker(phi).
typical_uses: Verify maps defined on residue classes.
Construct evaluation and reduction maps from quotient rings.
common_misuses: Checking that I is an ideal but not that phi vanishes on I.
Assuming the induced map preserves identity when the convention for ring homomorphisms does not require it.
bridge_lemmas: Equal cosets differ by an element of I.
The induced kernel is ker(phi)/I.
repair_templates: Show phi(i)=0 for every i in I before defining the map on cosets.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Ideal correspondence for quotient rings
statement: Ideals of R/I correspond bijectively and inclusion-preservingly to ideals of R containing I.
conditions: I is a two-sided ideal of R.
pi:R->R/I is the quotient map.
conclusion: J maps to J/I and K maps to pi^{-1}(K), giving inverse bijections between ideals J containing I and ideals K of R/I; sums, intersections, and inclusions are preserved.
typical_uses: Classify ideals in a quotient ring.
Transfer maximality or primality questions to ideals above I.
common_misuses: Using J/I when J does not contain I.
Claiming all ideals of R correspond to ideals of R/I.
bridge_lemmas: Preimages of ideals under ring homomorphisms are ideals.
The quotient map is surjective.
repair_templates: Restrict attention to ideals containing I and apply image/preimage under the quotient map.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Exactness means image equals kernel
statement: A sequence of module homomorphisms is exact at a term precisely when the image of the incoming map equals the kernel of the outgoing map.
conditions: A--f->B--g->C is a sequence of module homomorphisms with g composed with f equal to zero.
conclusion: The sequence is exact at B if and only if im(f)=ker(g).
typical_uses: Expose the two separate containments hidden in an exactness claim.
Check short exact sequence arguments.
common_misuses: Proving only g composed with f=0, which gives im(f) contained in ker(g).
Confusing exactness with injectivity or surjectivity at every term.
bridge_lemmas: Exactness at the first nonzero term means injectivity.
Exactness at the last nonzero term means surjectivity.
repair_templates: After proving the zero composite, prove every element of ker(g) has a preimage under f.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Nakayama lemma over a local ring
statement: If M is a finitely generated module over a commutative local ring (R,m) and mM=M, then M=0.
conditions: R is a commutative local ring with maximal ideal m.
M is a finitely generated R-module.
mM=M.
conclusion: M is the zero module.
typical_uses: Lift generators of M/mM to generators of M.
Turn equality modulo the maximal ideal into a generation statement.
common_misuses: Omitting finite generation.
Replacing the Jacobson-radical or local maximal-ideal hypothesis by an arbitrary ideal.
bridge_lemmas: A matrix congruent to the identity modulo m has determinant outside m and hence is invertible.
repair_templates: Verify finite generation and that the ideal lies in the Jacobson radical before applying Nakayama.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Subfields of a finite field
statement: The field with p^n elements contains a unique subfield with p^d elements exactly for the positive divisors d of n.
conditions: p is prime.
n and d are positive integers.
F is a field with p^n elements.
conclusion: F has a subfield of order p^d if and only if d divides n, and such a subfield is unique inside F.
typical_uses: Check proposed finite-field inclusions.
Identify fixed fields of powers of Frobenius.
common_misuses: Inferring an inclusion merely from p^d being numerically smaller than p^n.
Forgetting that finite fields of a fixed order are unique only up to isomorphism unless embedded in a common field.
bridge_lemmas: The roots of x^(p^d)-x form the unique field of p^d elements in an algebraic closure.
p^d-1 divides p^n-1 when d divides n.
repair_templates: Replace the size comparison by the divisibility check d|n and identify the Frobenius fixed field.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Long exact sequence in cohomology
statement: A short exact sequence of cochain complexes induces a natural long exact sequence of cohomology groups joined by connecting homomorphisms.
conditions: 0->A->B->C->0 is degreewise short exact and the maps commute with the differentials.
conclusion: There is an exact sequence 0->H^0(A)->H^0(B)->H^0(C)->H^1(A)->H^1(B)->H^1(C)->H^2(A)->....
typical_uses: Transfer vanishing between complexes.
Locate an obstruction as a connecting class.
common_misuses: Applying the result to a sequence not exact in every degree.
Assuming the connecting map is zero without justification.
bridge_lemmas: A cocycle lift has differential in the image of the preceding complex, defining the connecting class.
repair_templates: Verify degreewise exactness and chain-map compatibility before invoking the long exact sequence.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Ext vanishing criteria for projective and injective modules
statement: A module P is projective exactly when Ext^1_R(P,B)=0 for every B, and Q is injective exactly when Ext^1_R(A,Q)=0 for every A; in either case all positive higher Ext groups vanish in the indicated variable.
conditions: R is a ring.
All objects are R-modules with compatible sidedness.
conclusion: Projectivity and injectivity are characterized by the corresponding universal Ext^1 vanishing conditions.
typical_uses: Detect splitting of short exact sequences.
Repair an unjustified lifting or extension step.
common_misuses: Checking Ext against only one test module.
Putting a projective module in the second Ext variable or an injective module in the first.
bridge_lemmas: Ext^1_R(N,L) classifies extensions of N by L.
repair_templates: Place the candidate module in the correct Ext variable and prove vanishing for every module.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Tor criterion for flatness
statement: A right R-module D is flat exactly when Tor^R_1(D,B)=0 for every left R-module B; equivalently all positive Tor groups in that variable vanish.
conditions: R is a ring.
D is a right R-module.
conclusion: Tensoring with D preserves injections exactly when the stated Tor groups vanish.
typical_uses: Check whether tensoring preserves a short exact sequence.
Identify failure of left exactness by Tor_1.
common_misuses: Assuming tensor product is always left exact.
Ignoring left-right module compatibility over a noncommutative ring.
bridge_lemmas: Tensor product is always right exact.
The Tor long exact sequence places Tor_1 before the tensor of the left term.
repair_templates: Prove D is flat or show Tor_1 vanishes before preserving injectivity under tensor.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Ext one classifies module extensions
statement: Ext^1_R(N,L) is in bijection with equivalence classes of short exact sequences 0->L->M->N->0, with zero corresponding to split extensions.
conditions: L and N are R-modules.
conclusion: An extension splits exactly when its class in Ext^1_R(N,L) is zero.
typical_uses: Translate a splitting problem into a cohomology calculation.
Distinguish equivalent from merely isomorphic middle modules.
common_misuses: Reversing L and N.
Treating isomorphic middle modules as automatically equivalent extensions.
bridge_lemmas: Equivalence of extensions requires a commuting diagram inducing the identity on L and N.
repair_templates: Construct the extension class with the variables in quotient-then-submodule order and test whether it is zero.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite group order annihilates positive cohomology
statement: For a finite group G and any G-module A, multiplication by |G| annihilates H^n(G,A) for every n>0; hence these groups vanish when multiplication by |G| is invertible on A.
conditions: G is finite.
A is a G-module.
n is positive.
conclusion: |G| H^n(G,A)=0; if |G| acts invertibly on A, then H^n(G,A)=0.
typical_uses: Prove coprime group extensions split.
Detect torsion restrictions on cohomology.
common_misuses: Including degree zero, where invariants need not vanish.
Concluding vanishing from annihilation without invertibility or coprimality.
bridge_lemmas: Restriction followed by corestriction is multiplication by the subgroup index.
repair_templates: Separate the annihilation conclusion from vanishing and verify that |G| is invertible on the coefficient module.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Second cohomology classifies extensions
statement: For a fixed action of G on an abelian group A, H^2(G,A) classifies equivalence classes of extensions of G by A inducing that action; the zero class corresponds to a split semidirect product.
conditions: A is an abelian G-module.
Only extensions inducing the specified G-action on A are compared.
conclusion: The extension splits exactly when its H^2 class is zero.
typical_uses: Diagnose a missing splitting argument.
Classify group laws on extensions through factor sets.
common_misuses: Ignoring the induced action on A.
Assuming all extensions split because A is abelian.
bridge_lemmas: Associativity of an extension factor set is the 2-cocycle identity.
Changing a section changes the factor set by a coboundary.
repair_templates: Fix the action, compute the factor-set class, and prove that it is a coboundary before claiming a complement exists.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Equivalent choice principles
statement: Over Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, Zorn's lemma, the axiom of choice, and the well-ordering principle are equivalent.
conditions: The usual axioms of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory are assumed.
conclusion: Any one of the three principles may be used to derive the other two.
typical_uses: Justify maximal-object arguments such as existence of bases or maximal ideals.
Recognize when a proof invokes choice implicitly.
common_misuses: Applying Zorn without proving every chain has an upper bound in the poset.
Confusing a maximal element with a greatest element.
bridge_lemmas: The union of a chain often supplies its upper bound, but must remain in the poset.
repair_templates: Specify the nonempty poset, verify upper bounds for all chains, and only then select a maximal element.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Determinant criterion for invertibility
statement: For a square matrix over a field, nonzero determinant, invertibility, full rank, trivial kernel, and linear independence of the columns are equivalent.
conditions: A is an n by n matrix over a field F.
conclusion: det(A) is nonzero if and only if A defines an automorphism of F^n, equivalently rank(A)=n and ker(A)=0.
typical_uses: Convert an invertibility claim into a scalar calculation.
Repair a uniqueness proof by proving the relevant determinant is nonzero.
common_misuses: Using the criterion for a nonsquare matrix.
Treating a nonzero determinant over a general commutative ring as enough unless it is a unit.
bridge_lemmas: A adj(A)=det(A)I.
Over a field a square map is injective exactly when surjective.
repair_templates: Check squareness and the coefficient ring; over a ring require det(A) to be a unit.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Dimension of an annihilator
statement: For a subspace W of a finite-dimensional vector space V, its annihilator W^0 in V* has dimension dim(V)-dim(W), and the double annihilator identifies with W under V congruent to V**.
conditions: V is finite-dimensional over a field.
W is a subspace of V.
conclusion: dim(W^0)=dim(V)-dim(W) and (W^0)^0=W under the canonical bidual identification.
typical_uses: Count independent linear constraints.
Repair dual-space containment arguments.
common_misuses: Using dimension subtraction without finite dimensionality.
Identifying V with V** without noting the canonical map and its finite-dimensional surjectivity.
bridge_lemmas: A basis of W extends to a basis of V and yields a dual basis.
repair_templates: Add finite dimensionality or replace the dimension claim by the always-valid canonical inclusion.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Field criterion for straightedge-compass constructibility
statement: A real number is straightedge-compass constructible from a base field F exactly when it lies in a tower of real field extensions of successive degree at most two; consequently an algebraic constructible element has degree a power of two over F.
conditions: F is the field of initially available coordinates in R.
Only ideal straightedge and compass operations are allowed.
conclusion: Constructibility is equivalent to membership in a quadratic tower, and algebraic constructibility forces [F(alpha):F] to divide a power of two.
typical_uses: Prove impossibility of classical constructions.
Repair geometric arguments by translating operations into field extensions.
common_misuses: Claiming every element of degree a power of two is constructible without a suitable quadratic tower or normal-closure condition.
Ignoring the starting field.
bridge_lemmas: Intersections of allowed lines and circles solve linear or quadratic equations over the current coordinate field.
repair_templates: Exhibit the quadratic tower for sufficiency, or show the element degree has an odd factor for impossibility.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Prime ideals under localization
statement: Prime ideals of D^{-1}R correspond bijectively to prime ideals of R disjoint from the multiplicative set D, by extension and contraction.
conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity.
D is a multiplicatively closed subset containing 1 and not 0.
conclusion: P maps to D^{-1}P and Q maps to its contraction, giving inverse inclusion-preserving correspondences between primes P disjoint from D and primes Q of D^{-1}R.
typical_uses: Describe Spec of a localization.
Reduce a global ideal problem to a local ring.
common_misuses: Localizing a prime that meets D and still treating its extension as proper.
Assuming all ideals, rather than saturated ideals, correspond by extension-contraction.
bridge_lemmas: An element r/1 lies in D^{-1}P exactly when dr lies in P for some d in D.
repair_templates: Verify P intersect D is empty before extending it and use contraction to recover the original prime.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite module criterion for integrality
statement: For an R-algebra S generated by finitely many elements, S is integral over R exactly when S is finitely generated as an R-module.
conditions: R is a commutative ring with identity.
S=R[s_1,...,s_n] is a finitely generated R-algebra.
conclusion: Every element of S is integral over R if and only if S is module-finite over R.
typical_uses: Prove transitivity of integrality.
Turn monic polynomial relations into a finite spanning set.
common_misuses: Dropping finite algebra generation in the reverse direction.
Using an arbitrary polynomial relation instead of a monic one.
bridge_lemmas: Powers above the degree of a monic relation reduce to lower powers.
The determinant trick produces a monic annihilating polynomial.
repair_templates: Show the algebra has finitely many generators and that each is integral, then span by bounded monomials.

source: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Yoneda determination by morphisms
statement: An object is determined up to unique isomorphism by its representable Hom functor: a natural isomorphism Hom(-,A) congruent to Hom(-,B), or covariantly Hom(A,-) congruent to Hom(B,-), induces an isomorphism A congruent to B.
conditions: A and B are objects of a locally small category.
The stated Hom functors are naturally isomorphic.
conclusion: A and B are isomorphic, with the isomorphism recovered from the image of an identity morphism.
typical_uses: Prove uniqueness of universal constructions.
Repair claims that two objects are canonical merely because their underlying sets correspond.
common_misuses: Using pointwise bijections that are not natural.
Concluding literal equality instead of isomorphism.
bridge_lemmas: Naturality applied to identity morphisms makes the recovered arrows inverse.
repair_templates: Write the naturality square and evaluate the transformation and its inverse at identity maps.
